[USER] The user is looking for advice on fertilizing their herbs.  
[USER] The user has been using a general-purpose fertilizer for their herbs.  
[USER] The user is unsure if a general-purpose fertilizer is the best for their herbs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Herbs have unique fertilization needs, and using a general-purpose fertilizer may not provide them with the nutrients they require to thrive.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] General-purpose fertilizers often have high nitrogen levels, which can promote leaf growth at the expense of flavor and essential oil production in herbs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Herbs prefer a slightly acidic to neutral soil pH (around 6.0-7.0).  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Herbs require specific micronutrients like iron, zinc, and manganese, which might be lacking in general-purpose fertilizers.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] A balanced fertilizer with a ratio of 5-5-5 or 10-10-10 is suitable for most herbs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Opt for a fertilizer that is pH-balanced or slightly acidic to maintain the optimal pH range for herbs.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Look for fertilizers that contain micronutrients like iron, zinc, manganese, and copper, which are essential for herb growth and flavor development.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Consider using organic or natural fertilizers, as they tend to release nutrients slowly and promote healthy soil microbiology.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Recommended fertilizers include Miracle-Gro Shake 'n Feed All Purpose Plant Food, Espoma Organic Herb Tone Fertilizer, E.B. Stone Organics Herb & Vegetable Fertilizer, and fish emulsion or compost tea.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Fertilize sparingly; herbs don't require a lot of fertilizer.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Test your soil periodically to determine its pH and nutrient levels.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Fertilizers work best when the soil is consistently moist but not waterlogged.  
[USER] The user has been using tap water for their herb plants.  
[USER] The user is asking if it is okay to use tap water or if they should switch to rainwater or filtered water.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Using tap water for herb plants is generally okay, but it may not always be the best option.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Pros of tap water include convenience and cost-effectiveness.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Cons of tap water include chlorine and chloramines, mineral buildup, and potential pH imbalance.
